h1:
Saraburi Sunflower Fields
Golden Season Late Rains to Winter
intro: When the first cool breeze rolls in, vast swathes of Saraburi turn solid gold. Tens of thousands of sunflowers tilt east to catch the morning light all at once — and it's exactly the kind of scene Bangkok residents drive out early for, snap a few hundred photos, then head home before lunch. We've pulled together the real locations that are actually open to visitors, the bloom windows that actually hold, the exact time of morning the light is worth waking up for, and the routes to get there.

blocks.html: Sunflowers are a post-harvest crop that farmers across several Saraburi districts have grown for years — they're low-maintenance in the dry season and good for the soil. When the rains wind down and temperatures drop, these fields bloom together into a sea of yellow, turning into a seasonal stop for people on the way to Khao Yai or Lopburi. What makes Saraburi stand out is how spread out the fields are: Phra Phutthabat, Wang Muang, Kaeng Khoi, Muak Lek, Nong Don — you can pick whichever district suits your route.

blocks.text: When Do the Saraburi Sunflowers Bloom?

blocks.html: The main bloom window is mid-November through January every year. Farmers stagger their plantings across several rounds so there are flowers blooming continuously. The first round typically peaks late November to early December, with another round following from late December through late January. Any given field is at its best for only about 7–10 days before the flowers start to droop — so always check the field's Facebook page or a Saraburi travel group for current photos before you drive out, or you might find it already harvested.

blocks.title: Check before you go
blocks.html: Fields don't peak at the same time — some are in full bloom early in the month, others later. Search the field name on Facebook or look for recent posts tagged #ทุ่งทานตะวันสระบุรี to get live photos showing which fields are currently at their best.

Saraburi's sunflower fields aren't concentrated in one place — they're scattered across districts where farmers grow post-harvest crops. Each area has a different feel: some are wide fields right alongside the road, others are near other attractions worth visiting back-to-back. Pick based on the route you're already taking.

items.name: Wang Muang District
items.blurb: The district with the largest total sunflower acreage in the province. Wide fields along the Phatthana Nikhom–Wang Muang road, close to Pasak Jolasid Dam — easy to combine both in one trip.

items.name: Phra Phutthabat District
items.blurb: Fields spread across farmland around Phra Phutthabat town. Pairs well with Wat Phra Phutthabat and the famous Dok Mai Tak Bat (flower alms) offering — both doable in a single day.

items.name: Kaeng Khoi District (Ban Hin Son)
items.blurb: The Ban Hin Son sunflower field in Tambon Ta Liao / Tambon Taeng is set up properly for visitors — walking paths, photo spots, and a ~20 THB entry fee.

items.name: Muak Lek District
items.blurb: Smaller fields scattered across farms. Easy to follow up with a dairy farm visit and a mountain café. A good pick if you want to avoid the bigger crowds.

blocks.html: There are also smaller fields in Nong Don, Nong Khae, and Chaloem Phra Kiat districts planted by local families on their own land. Most don't charge entry, but please walk carefully — don't step on the plants — and take your rubbish home.

blocks.text: Best Time of Day for Photos

blocks.html: The key to photographing sunflowers is that they track the sun. In the morning they face east, so if you arrive early and stand with the sun behind you, you'll get flowers looking straight into the lens with soft, even light. As the morning wears on and the sun climbs, the flowers follow — and the angle shifts.

items: Best window — around 7:30–9:30 a.m. Gentle morning light, flowers angled toward you, not yet hot, far fewer people.
Where to stand — face west with the sun at your back. The flowers will be looking straight at your camera.
Avoid midday — harsh light, flowers turned away from you, heavy shadows, hotter, and noticeably more crowded.
Late afternoon (4:00–5:30 p.m.) — warm golden tones are nice, but flowers will be facing away from most positions; you'll need to work harder to find a good angle.

blocks.title: Shot tips that actually work
blocks.html: Get low — bring your lens down to flower level and shoot so you see rows of sunflowers receding into the distance. It makes the field look deep and dense. For portraits, wear something that contrasts with yellow: white, blue, or red will pop against the background.

blocks.text: Entry Fees and What to Know Before You Go

items: Entry fee — usually 10–20 THB per person. The money goes to buying seeds for the next planting round and maintaining the field.
Opening hours — organised fields typically open around 6:00 a.m.–6:00 p.m., but morning is by far the best time.
Getting there — drive from Bangkok on Phahon Yothin Road (Highway 1), about 2–2.5 hours to Saraburi, then branch off to whichever district you're visiting.
No car? — Take a coach or minivan to Saraburi town, then hire a local driver or charter a songthaew (shared pickup truck) to reach the fields.
What to bring — hat, sunscreen, water, shoes that can handle dirt paths, and cash for the entry fee and any food stalls at the field entrance.

blocks.title: Honest heads-up
blocks.html: These are working farms, not manicured garden attractions. Some years rain, pests, or heat means the flowers don't look as spectacular as those photos from five seasons ago that keep circulating online. Set your expectations based on the most recent photos from this season — that's the only benchmark that matters.

blocks.text: Where to Head After the Sunflowers

blocks.html: One advantage of Saraburi's sunflower fields is how close they are to other things worth seeing. Once you've finished shooting by mid-morning, you still have half a day left to fill.

items.name: Pasak Jolasid Dam
items.blurb: Close to the Wang Muang fields. The dam has a long scenic crest road and a tram tour. In winter there's a market along the waterfront and the air is noticeably cooler.

items.name: Wat Phra Phutthabat
items.blurb: Saraburi's most revered temple, enshrining a footprint of the Buddha. Combine it with the sunflower fields in the Phra Phutthabat district — both are in the same area.

items.name: Muak Lek Dairy Farm
items.blurb: Feed the cows, try fresh milk and ice cream. A good family-friendly stop after the Muak Lek sunflower fields — kids enjoy it.

faq.q: When do the Saraburi sunflower fields bloom?
faq.a: The main bloom window is mid-November through January — the transition from rainy to cool season. Farmers plant in multiple rounds to keep flowers coming continuously. The first round usually peaks late November to early December, with another following late December to January. Each individual field is at its best for only about 7–10 days, so check recent photos before you go.

faq.q: What time of day is best for photographing the sunflowers?
faq.a: Around 7:30–9:30 a.m. is ideal. In the morning sunflowers face east to catch the light, so stand with the sun behind you and shoot west — the flowers will be facing the camera in soft, flattering light. It's also cooler and less crowded at that hour.

faq.q: How much is the entry fee for Saraburi's sunflower fields?
faq.a: Most fields charge around 10–20 THB per person. The money goes toward buying seeds for the next season and maintaining the field. Some smaller family-operated plots don't charge anything. Bring cash — card readers are rarely available at field entrances.

faq.q: Which districts in Saraburi have sunflower fields?
faq.a: Fields are spread across several districts. Wang Muang has the largest total area; Phra Phutthabat, Kaeng Khoi (Ban Hin Son), and Muak Lek are the other main zones. Smaller plots also exist in Nong Don, Nong Khae, and Chaloem Phra Kiat. Choose based on which district is on your route.

faq.q: How do you get to the Saraburi sunflower fields from Bangkok?
faq.a: Drive north on Phahon Yothin Road (Highway 1) — Saraburi is about 2–2.5 hours from Bangkok, then branch off to whichever district you're heading to. Without a car, take a coach or minivan to Saraburi town and hire a local driver or charter a songthaew to reach the fields.
